title: Sound, good, weak
hook: hadith are graded: sahih, hasan, da'if, and fabricated

segments.voice: Yesterday, the matn, the text itself, and your line: the words are tested too. Did you read a quote once with the name taken off? Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

After report upon report in his collection, al-Tirmidhi does something you can see right on the page. He steps out from behind the book and gives his own verdict. Abu Isa said, he writes, using the name he went by: this hadith is hasan sahih. Or: this hadith is gharib, rare, and we know it only through this chain. It's like a teacher writing a note in the margin of the exam he's handing you. The report, and then a grade. Chains and texts have been weighed for days now on this path. Today, the words for what the weighing finds. Today, sahih.
screen: `AL-TIRMIDHI STEPS OUT.` → `HIS OWN VERDICT.` → `A REPORT, AND A GRADE.`

segments.voice: First, sahih. It means sound, healthy, whole. In the definition laid out by Ibn al-Salah, a sound hadith has a connected chain, every link meeting the next. Every narrator is upright in character and precise in memory. And the report is free of two hidden problems: oddness, where it goes against what more reliable narrators report, and a concealed defect that only careful comparison reveals. Second, hasan. Good. Close to sound, but a narrator's precision is a step lighter: honest, but not quite as sharp. Scholars of law still act on a good hadith. Third, da'if. Weak. Something in the conditions is missing. A gap in the chain. A narrator nobody can vouch for. A memory known to wander. Weak doesn't mean false. It means not established. Scholars differ on whether, and how, a weak report may be used for encouragement, and we'll come back to that later this block. Fourth, the floor below weak. Mawdu': fabricated. That isn't a grade of the Prophet's words at all. It's a forgery, words put in his mouth, and scholars named it so it couldn't hide among the others. Two more things belong in the picture. Grades can differ: one scholar may call a report good where another calls it weak, and both show their reasons. And Shia hadith scholarship has its own grading terms, some with the same names, weighed by its own conditions. So a grade isn't a stamp from nowhere. It's a scholar's judgment, with the work showing.
screen: `SAHIH: SOUND, CHAIN UNBROKEN.` · `HASAN: GOOD, A STEP LIGHTER.` · `DA'IF: WEAK, NOT ESTABLISHED.` · `MAWDU': A FORGERY.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn the grade of a hadith you know. Settle, and breathe. Choose one saying of the Prophet you've heard more than once. Maybe from this path, maybe from a parent, a sermon, a poster. Say it to yourself. Now ask: do I know its grade? Do I know which collection it's in? If you do, hold that for a moment. If you don't, that's the gap to notice. Decide where you'll look: a teacher you trust, a printed collection, or a reference that shows the grade beside the text. If you pray, you can ask to carry only what's sound. The bell holds the time.
Sahih. Sound: an unbroken chain of upright, precise narrators, with no oddness and no hidden defect. Beside it, hasan, good, and da'if, weak. Today's word.
Your line: graded with care. Today, look up the grade of the hadith you chose, or ask someone who would know. Tomorrow: many chains. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Hadith scholars grade reports as sahih (sound), hasan (good) or da'if (weak), and identify fabricated ones; modern editions of the collections often print a scholar's grade beside each report, and Shia scholarship uses its own grading terms.

fork.setup: you're grading a report. every narrator is honest and sharp, but one of them never met the man he quotes. what grade?
fork.reveal: a sound hadith needs a connected chain. a missing link makes it weak, not fabricated: honest people, a gap between them.

original.note: sound, healthy, whole: the highest grade of a single report.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hadith is either real or fake.
what it means: hadith are graded: sound, good, weak, and below them, fabricated.
what a scholar hears: Ibn al-Salah's conditions: a connected chain, upright and precise narrators, no oddness, no hidden defect.

notes: Ibn al-Salah's definition of sahih (connected chain, 'adl and dabit narrators, no shudhudh, no 'illah) summarized; confirm. 'Whose handbook later scholars built on' is a general claim; soften if needed.
Al-Tirmidhi's verdicts ('Abu Isa said: this hadith is hasan sahih'; 'gharib, we know it only through this chain'): confirm phrasing.
Hasan described as a narrator 'a step lighter' in precision: the standard later definition; confirm.
'Scholars of law still act on a good hadith': general; confirm.
Shia grading terms (e.g. sahih, hasan, muwaththaq, da'if) mentioned without detail; confirm phrasing.
